description:
We’re Thermal Twins! , Two devs tackling NASA Space Apps’ MODIS + VIIRS Hot Spots Harmonization challenge. 

Two satellites, decades of fire data that doesn’t quite match. We’re building an interactive web map that puts both sensors on equal footing. 

Looking for teammates with GIS, remote sensing, Python or frontend skills. If you like turning messy satellite data into something people can actually use, message us!
summary:
Satellites don’t all see fire the same way. MODIS and VIIRS pick up hotspots differently, so putting their raw counts side by side can be misleading. That’s the problem we built Thermal Twins to tackle.

We take NASA FIRMS active-fire data and build a sensor-aware historical record, then harmonize the two sensors so comparisons across time and regions hold up. Open the map, pick any area, and see how it has burned over the years. You can check how current activity compares to its historical baseline, and explore trends through calendar and analytical views.

We also show our harmonized results next to a naive sensor splice, so you can see exactly what goes wrong when you treat both sensors as interchangeable. Our approach accounts for uncertainty and is tested on held-out data, so we’re not just assuming it works.

Our goal is to make long-term satellite fire data easier to explore and understand, and to be honest about what hotspot data can and can’t tell us.
details:
The Problem

Satellite fire-monitoring systems give us valuable information about active fires and thermal anomalies. But different instruments don’t observe the Earth in quite the same way. MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution, observation characteristics, and detection behaviour, so simply combining their raw hotspot counts can introduce artificial changes into a historical record.

This makes it hard to tell whether fire activity has genuinely changed or whether the observing sensor has.

Our Solution: Thermal Twins

Thermal Twins is an interactive platform for exploring sensor-aware, harmonized satellite fire observations. It uses NASA FIRMS active-fire data from MODIS and VIIRS to give users a consistent analytical experience across historical periods and geographic regions.

With Thermal Twins, users can:

  • Explore historical fire activity on an interactive map.
  • Switch between supported regions, including India and Argentina.
  • Select preset regions or draw their own areas of interest using bounding boxes and polygons.
  • Choose date ranges and historical baseline years.
  • Explore monthly and seasonal patterns through an interactive burning calendar.
  • Examine trends and compare current activity against historical reference periods.
  • Compare harmonized observations with a naive sensor-splicing approach to see the effect of sensor differences.
  • Inspect analytical summaries and download data for further exploration.

How It Works

The data pipeline retrieves both historical and near-real-time active-fire observations from NASA FIRMS. These observations are cleaned, standardized, and processed while keeping track of which sensor each one came from.

MODIS and VIIRS are treated as distinct measurement sources, not as interchangeable counts. The harmonization workflow applies sensor-aware processing and is evaluated using held-out data and uncertainty-aware methods.

Results are presented through interactive geographic and temporal visualizations, so users can see how their interpretation of fire activity changes once sensor differences are accounted for, instead of relying on a simple concatenation of satellite records.

Why It Matters

A long-term fire record can be misleading if a change in satellite instruments is mistaken for a change in fire activity. Thermal Twins brings this issue into view and gives users the tools to explore historical patterns with more context.

The platform is meant to be an exploratory and analytical resource for understanding satellite-observed fire activity. It does not claim to identify individual fires from hotspot detections, nor does it replace ground-based verification or operational fire-monitoring systems.

Technology Stack

  • Data source: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations
  • Data processing: Python and analytical data-processing pipelines
  • Geospatial processing: H3 hexagonal spatial indexing
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS
  • Mapping: MapLibre GL JS
  • Charts and visual analytics: Apache ECharts
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Version control: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Design Decisions

The central idea behind Thermal Twins is to make two different satellite observation systems comparable without hiding their differences. The harmonized-versus-naive comparison lets users see for themselves what sensor transitions do to a record.

We also made transparency a priority. Sensor provenance, historical baselines, uncertainty, and limitations are built into the experience rather than tucked away. The interface brings geographic exploration, temporal analysis, and comparative evaluation together in one place.

Our goal isn’t just to show where hotspots were detected but to help users understand what a multi-sensor historical fire record can and can't tell us.
projectRefs: H3 – Uber Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index
